solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Very strong players joining club

blocks.note: The players in a play are its cast.
An iron is a golf club.

explanation.surface: A band of formidable players signs up with a club.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes a sports team of the players and the club; in the wordplay they are a theatre company and a golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: the metal is hard and rigid, so the adjective describes anything firm and unbreakable, like a guarantee or an alibi.

clue.text: Say law needs changing continually

indicators.note: The letters of 'say law' need changing into a new order.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: A campaigner insists a law must be reformed over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like the verb introducing a claim, but it is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean at all times, without a break.

clue.text: Support upcoming boy with record set out on opposite course

indicators.note: In a down clue, letters coming up read from bottom to top.

blocks.note: To back is to support.
A lad is a boy.
An EP is an extended-play record.

explanation.surface: Someone backs a young lad who is releasing a record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upcoming' reads as 'up-and-coming' about the boy; in a down clue it turns the boy and the record upward together.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: turning a bicycle's pedals backward reverses it, so the verb means retreating from a position or heading the other way.

clue.text: Eat away at metal bar in centre

indicators.note: The bar is placed in the centre.

blocks.note: A rod is a metal bar.
The core is the centre.

explanation.surface: Rust gnaws at a metal bar from its middle outward.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'metal bar in centre' as one picture of rust from the inside; 'centre' is really a separate piece of wordplay that holds the bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: rust and acid wear metal away gradually, which is exactly what this verb describes.

clue.text: Biting fast

blocks.note: Weather that bites is sharply cold.
Quick and agile, as a small car might be.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Biting fast' suggests a dog that snaps quickly; it is two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: a chilly wind is described this way, and so is a small car that darts through traffic.

clue.text: Richard taking root, say, as all-powerful ruler

indicators.note: 'Say' asks for the words as spoken.

blocks.note: Dick is short for Richard.
A tater is a potato, a root vegetable in slang.

explanation.surface: A man named Richard takes root and becomes a tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: Tater is informal for potato; put Richard's nickname in front and say the pair out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the title comes from Roman magistrates granted absolute power in emergencies, and now means any autocrat.

clue.text: Biblical food reportedly in fashion

indicators.note: 'Reportedly' means as it is heard said.

blocks.note: Manna fed the Israelites in the wilderness.

explanation.surface: Manna from the Bible is said to be trendy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In fashion' reads as trendy, but 'fashion' alone is the definition, as in 'after a fashion'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'in this fashion' and 'in this way' show both nouns mean a way of doing something.

clue.text: What Lisa might do when at sea

definitions.text: What Lisa might do when at sea

indicators.note: Letters at sea are confused and out of order.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: A woman named Lisa on a boat trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, and the same words also scramble the name into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: &lit: the whole clue reads straight, since a woman out on the water in a yacht would naturally be doing just that.

clue.text: Jack’s novel concerning the old people down under

definitions.text: concerning the old people down under

blocks.note: Jack and AB (able seaman) are both sailors.
Something novel is original.

explanation.surface: A writer called Jack has published a book about Australia's first peoples.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack's novel' looks like a book by Jack; Jack is a sailor and 'novel' is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective for the first peoples of Australia; 'down under' is informal for Australia and 'old' means there first.

clue.text: Raider‘s destroyed cake with tart being thrown around

indicators.note: A destroyed cake has its letters wrecked.
Tart being thrown sends its letters flying.
The thrown tart goes around the destroyed cake.

blocks.note: Anagram fodder that forms the outside.
Anagram fodder that goes inside.

explanation.surface: An intruder wrecks a cake while a tart gets flung about.
explanation.walkthrough: Each pastry is scrambled on its own, and only then does 'around' put one inside the other; it is not one big anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a raider is someone who makes a sudden assault.

clue.text: Old man needing shelter — that’s obvious

blocks.note: Pa is father, the old man.
A tent is a shelter.

explanation.surface: An elderly man clearly needs a roof over his head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' is a familiar term for one's father.
explanation.definitionFit: A less familiar sense: apart from the inventor's licence, the adjective means plain to see, as in a flagrant lie.

clue.text: Increase in noise as soccer gets played round goal

indicators.note: Soccer being played sends its letters in a new order.
The rearranged soccer goes round the goal.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.
A goal is an end, an aim.

explanation.surface: The crowd gets louder as a football match is played and a goal goes in.
explanation.walkthrough: In the surface 'goal' is a score; in the wordplay it is an aim.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical term used in its general sense: a passage, or a roar, that grows steadily louder.

clue.text: Grim film you and I should leave

indicators.note: 'You and I' leaving the film means those letters are taken out.

blocks.note: A western is a cowboy film.
You and I together are we.

explanation.surface: A bleak film is so bad that you and I should walk out.
explanation.walkthrough: The film is a genre, not a title, and the pronoun comes off its front.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a severe, unsmiling face can be called grim or this equally.

clue.text: Her modest fancy will get stifled

indicators.note: A fancy version of the letters is an elaborate rearrangement.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: A shy woman's romantic wish will be suppressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' reads as a noun, a wish; here it is an adjective saying the letters are dressed up anew.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean suppressed, or deprived of air.

clue.text: Puzzler continued unnoticed to give an example

definitions.text: Puzzler continued unnoticed to give an example

blocks.note: Reads as a person who sets or solves puzzles; really a kind of word puzzle.
Reads as carrying on without being seen; really two words made from the same nine letters.
Says the pair just printed is itself a specimen of the puzzle meant.

explanation.surface: A puzzle-setter carried on without anyone noticing.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange 'continued' and you get 'unnoticed', so the clue shows its own answer in action.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: one word rearranged into another is exactly this kind of word puzzle.

clue.text: Visit High Street and let rip

blocks.note: A trip into the centre for the shops.
To act with great abandon or lavish spending.

explanation.surface: A shopper heads for the high street and goes on a spree.
explanation.walkthrough: A high street is the main shopping street of a British town.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: literally a trip into the centre, and idiomatically doing something lavishly and without restraint.

clue.text: States the woman may identify herself with I…

blocks.note: The ellipsis runs on: 'I …' is completed by the verb.
A woman's name that completes the introduction.

explanation.surface: A woman announces her identity with the word 'I'.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis asks you to finish 'I …' as a woman introducing herself might; drop the I and the rest is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The States' is everyday shorthand for the United States, the country as a whole.

clue.text: Understanding it’s infectious

blocks.note: Grasping a meaning, as in getting a joke.
Passed easily from one person to another.

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests insight spreads like a disease; the two words are separate senses of one answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: grasping what someone says, and describing a disease that passes easily between people.

clue.text: In fun, read Yeats, find yourself badly prepared

indicators.note: The answer sits in the run of words that follows.

blocks.note: fUN READ Yeats.

explanation.surface: Someone reads Yeats for pleasure and finds they are out of their depth.
explanation.walkthrough: W. B. Yeats is a famous Irish poet; the answer crosses the gaps between three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the prefix un- negates a word meaning prepared.

clue.text: Foam from really old tumble-drier, hot to start with

indicators.note: Take what each word starts with.

blocks.note: First letter.
First letter.
First letter.
First letter.
First letter.

explanation.surface: Suds pour out of an ancient tumble-drier that is running hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' looks like a link word, but it supplies the first letter too.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean a mass of small bubbles on a liquid.

clue.text: Story about right to intercept drug

indicators.note: Right cuts into the drug, landing inside it.

blocks.note: Re means about, concerning.
R is the abbreviation for right.
Pot is cannabis.

explanation.surface: A news story about the authorities having the right to seize drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right to intercept' reads as a legal power; in the wordplay the letter for right slips inside the slang word for cannabis.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the journalistic sense: a news item filed from the scene.

clue.text: Prompt soldier’s going west, getting aboard in Washington, say

indicators.note: In an across clue, going west means reading right to left.
Getting aboard puts the soldier inside.

blocks.note: A GI is an American soldier.
Taken as printed.
Washington is one example of a US state.

explanation.surface: A soldier heads west and boards a vessel in Washington.
explanation.walkthrough: In the surface 'in Washington' is a location; in the wordplay the little word is kept as letters, and Washington is just one example of its kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to spur someone into action or bring something about.

clue.text: One will stand between king and first lady to mourn

indicators.note: The one is set in line between the other two pieces.

blocks.note: GR is George Rex, King George.
I is the Roman numeral one.
Eve was the first woman in Genesis.

explanation.surface: Someone interposes between a king and his queen in their time of sorrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First lady' suggests a president's wife, but here it is the first woman of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to feel or show deep sorrow over a death or loss.

clue.text: Poetic creature’s ‘Boat Poles’ taking first place

indicators.note: The poles are put at the front of the boat.

blocks.note: The two poles are S (south) and N (north).
Noah's ark is a boat.

explanation.surface: A poem's creature is titled 'Boat Poles' and wins first prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' reads as punting poles or Polish people; it means the two ends of the earth's axis.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the imaginary beast hunted in Lewis Carroll's nonsense poem of 1876.

clue.text: Exact place ahead

blocks.note: A spot is a place.
On means onward, ahead.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Exact place' reads as one phrase; the first word alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A British informal idiom for exactly right, as a guess or an impression might be.

clue.text: Vision certainly is required in Boat Race crew

indicators.note: Certainly is required inside the crew.

blocks.note: Yes means certainly.
Each Boat Race crew is an eight, eight rowers.

explanation.surface: Rowers in the Boat Race need a clear view of where they are going.
explanation.walkthrough: The Boat Race is the annual Oxford-Cambridge rowing race on the Thames, raced in boats of eight.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name the faculty of seeing, though 'vision' also stretches to imagination.

clue.text: Stalemate, perhaps, with game’s castle defence

blocks.note: Stalemate in chess is one kind of draw.
Bridge is a card game.

explanation.surface: A chess stalemate becomes the game's way of defending the king's castle.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess words suggest castling; 'castle' here is a real fortress.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a span over a moat that can be raised to keep attackers out of a fortress.

clue.text: Very popular ordinary drink

blocks.note: V is the abbreviation for very.
In means fashionable, popular.
O is the abbreviation for ordinary.

explanation.surface: A well-loved everyday tipple.
explanation.walkthrough: Three short standard abbreviations in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: A borrowing: the Italian and Spanish word for wine, used in informal English for any glass of it.
